do a carfacts and look at consumer reports, you can get it free from your library. check for recalls. ofcourse test drive it and maybe even find a mechanic to give it a look over, some will do it for free even.

The seller will always say it was well maintained, rebuilt, etc etc but without documentation you should assume they're lying.

Look for rust under the car. People sometimes call it cancer because it doesn't go away. It doesn't spell immediate trouble but eventually it'll spread and put holes in your floor or your frame when it gets severe.

Look for different colored body parts or ones that sit skewed a little. This might mean it was hit and then replaced. You can pretty up the body but a bent frame means dangerous handling and frequent tire replacement.

Look for uneven wear on the tires, this might indicate something wrong with the suspension and possibly that it was crashed before.

Listen for chatter, rattling, and knocking (it'll sound like a rapid knock on the door) from the engine. This doesn't mean the engine is done for right away, but it means it won't last as long as you'd want.

When you drive, pay attention to if it feels like the car is chugging at all. This could be engine trouble but it could also be a slipping transmission. Both are expensive.

Definitely test drive the car. And if you know a bit about cars, always check it from top to bottom before you buy used. If you don't know a whole lot about them, take someone with you who does. The seller is only thinking about making a sell, and unless they are really decent people, they won't tell you about any problems the car might have. Make sure you know of any problem before handing over the cash.
Take it to a mechanic and have him go over it with diagnostic tools. Do a compression test.
Was going to say the same thing. Take it to your mechanic and have them check it out bumper to bumper. They should charge you $100 -$150, but money well spent.
This. I posted something lengthy below, but this is the best option if available.

Private sales: If you bring the cash, bring a friend. Be conscious of the state of the car when you see it, e.g. "the engine was warm before the test drive, is there an issue where you have to warm up the car for smooth operation?" Verse yourself in common issues that will be a headache down the road, e.g. is there an oil leak? Know enough to carry out a basic inspection on your own, e.g. tread depth on the tires, oil level which can be indicative of poor maintainance if low. Always drive the car a sufficient amount of time to get it to heat up and make sure it runs smoothly, e.g. does the transmission "slam", does it idle well.
Look for major repairs and ask about maintenance history. Then bring it to a mechanic you trust and have him look it over.

Don't let your enthusiasm for a new car, cloud your judgement. In person, people can seem really influential, and you can go against judgement you normally would hear. Take an adult you trust with you, and talk it over with them in private after the test drive. If it still looks like a winner, take it to the shop, and let them do a once over.

A friend of mine buys/sells high end used cars for fun (retired and wanted something to do). He takes a tool that measures the paint thickness. If the vehicle ever had repairs done the paint will be a different thickness. He can easily tell if the seller is trying to hide a repair job. Comes in handy.

Not to sounds like a shill, but I'd say to take a look at Carmax, if they have one in your area. Car dealerships, in general, have the worst salesmen you'll ever deal with. Carmax bases its entire reputation on making sure the cars are on the up-and-up, and they do charge extra for that, but they also back it up with great warranty options and guarantees that actually work, the downside being that you can't haggle on pricing. Their financing, however, is terrible, go to a local credit union for that.

When buying my last car we had a great experience at CarMax. They had the best pricing and we actually got great financing with a low interest rate and lower payment than we had anticipated (though I am sure this is dependent on your credit rating). Still, we did our research before hand, compared pricing, checked the Carfax, and did 2 test drives.

If you are trading a car in I would suggest shopping around at dealers before you actually intend to buy, so that you have a clear idea of what you should get for your trade when you do find the car you want to buy. But you must be committed to walk away without a car if you do this. They will do anything they can to keep you from leaving without a car. You will question yourself in the moment, but feel it will feel like a victory when all those sales tactics leave your brain and reason returns.

I have bought and sold many cars over the years and the main thing for me is how many Miles/Kms has the car done. The lower the better. Don't be fooled by some people claiming 'it doesn't matter' it does.
Get the vin number and run a full car fax report on it. Seriously. It'll tell you a lot about the car's history.

Good relationships are the most critical component of trouble-free car ownership.

 

Talk to your mechanic first. It is worth asking your local mechanic which brands they have the easiest time getting parts for, because they are perfectly entitled to charge you for their time if it takes a lot of work to source a part required for repair. If you ask any mechanic worth their salt for a shortlist (say 3 or 4 models) that would be suitable for your requirements and budget, they will be happy to take the time. Any mechanic who can't be bothered is not worth your time or money. You can trust most mechanics to recommend a reliable model because routine service & inspection work is the most profitable kind of work for them because they want to maximise the proportion of hours in the day spent on billable work. Long drawn out pain in the ass jobs make for good war stories but often involve a large amounts of non-billable time.

 

The second most important thing - Buy a popular economy car. While an economy car is far from being a guarantee of reliability, it tilts the odds much further in your favour. Also, the more common a model is, the more robust the supply chain will be for salvaged parts.

 

Thirdly, maintenance history is important. Cars have gotten way tougher over the years in terms of coping with abuse and they've often got even worse at coping with neglect. If a car comes without properly filled logbooks, just walk away. It's not even worth the time or money to get it inspected.

 

Fourth, once you've found something suitable, then take it to the mechanic you spoke with first and get them to do a full inspection and compression test. Whenever possible, you want the car to be inspected by the mechanic who is going to end up fixing it in the years to come.

Welcome to our first weekly topics! I've decided to divide these into two sections. 'Some Batty Biology' will visit a certain species or a certain facet of bats, such as echolocation or such. 'Humans Gone Batty' will visit the meet between man and these fascinating critters, by either fictional interpretations of them, conservation efforts, or other such things.

 

Some Batty Biology - The Ghost Faced Bat

After a little interest arose from the picture of one yesterday, I decided to give these guys a visit. There isn't much, but this is what could be found on the Ghost-Faced Bat! It's a species of microbat, which most notably means they use echolocation - megabats do not.

The Ghost-Faced Bat is a species largely found in Central American countries, as well as Mexico and southern parts of the United States. Due to this preference for warmer climates, they generally do not migrate in the winter, nor do they hibernate. There is speculation that there may be exceptions to this.

The bizarre appearance of their face comes in part from an underdeveloped nose. More on that here.

Generally speaking, this seems to be an understudied species, as several sources indicate the things we know about their seasonal movements and reproductive habits - among other things - are dubious at best.

 

Humans Gone Batty - Here's Some Words to Squeal About

So, you may have noticed the changes to the names of subscribers and viewers in our sidebar. I'm gonna take this bit to explain what those mean, as well as introduce some other bat-related phrases and language tidbits.

  • Flittermouse is simply an old word for bat, with roots in Germanic languages. Similarly to this, a number of languages draw similarities between mice and bats in their word for the latter.

  • Bats in the belfry is an older and kinda out-of-use phrase that has "crazy person" connotations similar to the term 'batty'. There's a fair few idioms that combine bats with crazy.

  • Blind as a bat is a fun one. Though it typically gets used to say someone or something can't see well, it isn't largely accurate in its comparison: a good number of bats actually see well enough outside of echolocation, and an entire grouping of bats - megabats - don't use echolocation at all.

  • Batshit crazy seems to have arisen from some odd combination of 'bullshit' and bats getting looped into crazy connotations. I've heard an urban legend that it came from the effects of guano on people, but after some double-checking, I think we can safely say that people are too batshit crazy to put that much effort into a saying.

 

That's all until next weekend! Next weekend we'll be looking at some different topics, hopefully interesting ones! I have some in the planning, but if there's something you'd like to see about, feel free to mention! Also, if I've gotten something wrong, please let me know - I'm learning about them too. ;)

Until next!
